title: The Desire Beneath the Ambition August 11, 2026
author: Kathleen Schafer
source: Extraordinarily Ordinary: A Field Guide for Being Human (kathleenschafer.substack.com),
summary: Kathleen Schafer reflects on launching a new men's leadership cohort, The Leaders' Companion, after five years running a similar program exclusively for women, and describes her surprise at how readily a room of accomplished men engaged with questions that went beyond career advancement. Rather than asking how to climb further, the men in the room wanted to know how to have a genuine positive impact on their communities while building a life that leaves room for presence, joy, and peace -- questions Schafer reads as evidence that raw ambition, left unexamined, can carry people a long way without ever telling them where they actually wanted to go. She introduces 'Desired Contribution' from her Leadership Connection Model as a reframing device: instead of asking what a person wants to accomplish, the question becomes what they want their life to make possible for others -- what gets a little better in a room, an organization, or a community because they are present. The essay closes with Schafer applying the same question to her own work, describing a shift in her own ambitions from producing more to clarifying what her work is actually meant to contribute.
points: Frames ambition as directionally neutral -- capable of building real skill and opportunity, but equally capable of carrying someone a long way without ever clarifying what the effort is actually for.

Introduces 'Desired Contribution' as a reframing tool that shifts the leadership question from achievement ('what do you want to become?') to consequence ('what becomes more possible for others because you are here?').

Uses her own experience launching a men's cohort after five years running a women's-only program to argue that the desire for meaningful contribution beneath ambition is not gender-specific, contrary to her own initial uncertainty.

Frames the difficulty as one of entanglement rather than corruption: ambition gets tangled up with approval, security, and recognition for understandable reasons, and the problem is pursuing those proxies long enough to forget what they were meant to produce.
quotes: They wanted space to consider who they were becoming. How they wanted to lead. How they could do meaningful work without allowing the work to consume them.

How do I actually have a positive impact on our deeply challenged communities? How do I do good in the world while also creating a life for my family, my partner, and myself that allows for presence, joy, and peace?

And yet ambition can carry us far without ever telling us where we actually want to go. Along the way, it can become entangled with many things. Approval. Security. Proving ourselves. Money. Recognition.
We are rarely asked: When you show up in a room, what gets a little better because you are there? Said another way: What becomes more possible for others because you are here?
As I enter a new season of my own work, I am thinking less about how much more I can produce and more about what I most want my work to contribute.
I do know that the desire beneath my ambition has become clearer. I am not seeking simply to do more. I want what I do to help create a better life together.
